notes:
Below is a verse‑by‑verse commentary on Psalm 86 (BSB), drawn entirely from the sources I could access. Where I could not locate a particular tradition’s view, I note that fact honestly.

---

## Title: “A Prayer of David”

The psalm is one of five in the Psalter specifically called a *Tephillah* (prayer). It is addressed so directly to God throughout that the title “prayer” is fitting, even though veins of praise run through it (Spurgeon). David uses the Hebrew word *Adonai* (“Master”) seven times, emphasising submission and God’s absolute lordship (Enduring Word).

**Sources:**
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-86/

---

## v. 1 — “Incline Your ear, O LORD, and answer me, for I am poor and needy.”

**Traditional reading:** David begins by asking God to “bow down” His ear — figurative language for God stooping from heaven to hear a humble plea. “Poor and needy” here means afflicted and miserable, not merely financially destitute. David appeals not to his own merit but to God’s compassion; misery is the “master argument with mercy” (Spurgeon). Calvin adds that nothing suits God’s nature more than to succour the afflicted, and the more destitute a person is of human help, the more inclined God is to help (Calvin).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** The phrase “poor and needy” means “doubly a son of poverty” — poor (without supply) and needy (full of wants but unable to supply them). Such reasoning would never be used by a proud man.

**Reformed (Calvin):** This prayer was dictated by the Holy Spirit for the poor and afflicted, so that despair may not overwhelm us in our greatest afflictions.

**Sources:**
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-86.html
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-86/

---

## v. 2 — “Preserve my soul, for I am godly. You are my God; save Your servant who trusts in You.”

**Traditional reading:** “I am godly” (KJV “holy”) is not a claim to sinless perfection. The psalmist means he is set apart for God, a recipient of God’s favour (*chasid*), and clear of the specific crimes his enemies charge him with. The Pulpit Commentary says David claims only “that sincerity in religion which God’s servants may rightly vindicate to themselves.” Spurgeon notes it is not self-righteousness for a good man to plead his innocence against false charges. Calvin stresses that David’s “meekness” toward his neighbours makes his enemies’ cruelty more odious. David immediately balances this by declaring his trust in God, lest anyone think he trusted in his own holiness.

**Reformed (Calvin):** Calvin translates “I am meek” and argues that David’s gentleness toward neighbours and his trust in God are the two arguments for divine help. Even the most virtuous pagans trusted in themselves, not God, and so perished.

**Sources:**
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/86.htm
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-86.html
- https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-86

---

## v. 3 — “Be merciful to me, O Lord, for I call to You all day long.”

**Traditional reading:** The verb “be merciful” (*chanan*) means “show favour” or “be gracious.” David appeals to nothing but mercy. “All day long” (or “daily”) shows persistent, importunate prayer. Spurgeon sees this as a holy pleading: if we have looked to the Lord alone in all former times, He will not desert us now.

**Sources:**
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/86.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-86.html

---

## v. 4 — “Bring joy to Your servant, for to You, O Lord, I lift up my soul.”

**Traditional reading:** Here the prayer rises from mere relief to a request for *gladness*. David counts God’s favour as his true wages. “Lifting up the soul” is a figure for turning the whole inner being toward God in trust, like the heliotrope turning to the sun (Spurgeon). The Pulpit Commentary notes that there is no more likely way to spiritual joy than always lifting the soul to God.

**Sources:**
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/86.htm

---

## v. 5 — “For You, O Lord, are kind and forgiving, rich in loving devotion to all who call on You.”

**Traditional reading:** This verse is widely recognised as David drawing on God’s self-revelation in Exodus 34:6–7. The rare Hebrew word *sallach* (“ready to forgive”) occurs only here. God is not merely willing to forgive eventually — He is *ready* to forgive *now*. His mercy is “plenteous” (abundant, not from a slender store). Spurgeon says David “seems to have stood in the cleft of the rock with Moses.”

**Reformed (Calvin):** It would not be enough for God to be good in general; He must also extend forgiving mercy to sinners. Calvin stresses that this plenteous mercy is restricted to “all who call upon Him,” excluding those who obstinately disregard God.

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik, Enduring Word):** Many wait to repent because they think time will make God more forgiving — but He is *ready* to forgive *now*. Meyer is quoted: “You have fallen a hundred times, and are ashamed to come to God again… But He will, for He is ready to forgive.”

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-86/
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-86.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/86.htm

---

## v. 6 — “Hear my prayer, O LORD, and attend to my plea for mercy.”

**Traditional reading:** This echoes v. 1. The psalmist begins afresh, asking God to give ear. The repetition is not “vain repetition” but earnest persistence, like a child crying with the same note over and over (Spurgeon). Even though God’s ear is always open, He listens *more favourably* when besought to listen (Pulpit).

**Sources:**
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/86.htm

---

## v. 7 — “In the day of my distress I call on You, because You answer me.”

**Traditional reading:** David expresses confident resolve: he *will* call because God *will* answer. Spurgeon argues that if prayer had no real effect, nobody would persist in it — but believers’ experience confirms that God really does aid those who call on Him. Calvin says David makes a particular application to himself of the truth just stated (that God is merciful to all who call).

**Sources:**
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-86.html

---

## v. 8 — “O Lord, there is none like You among the gods, nor any works like Yours.”

**Traditional reading:** “Among the gods” refers to the imaginary deities of the heathen (Baal, Dagon, etc.) — or possibly angelic beings or human rulers. The point is that no rival can compare with Jehovah in character or in deeds. The Pulpit Commentary and Spurgeon both note the reference to Exodus 15:11 (“Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods?”).

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** Even if every imaginary deity could become real, “yet would we choose Jehovah to be our God, and reject all others.”

**Reformed (Calvin):** David holds up all false gods to contempt and derision. He deliberately confines attention to God’s *works*, not abstract speculations about the divine essence, because God’s nature is infinitely above our understanding.

**Sources:**
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/86.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-86.html

---

## v. 9 — “All the nations You have made will come and bow before You, O Lord, and they will glorify Your name.”

**Traditional reading:** Because God made all nations (Acts 17:26), all nations will one day worship Him. This is a missionary, eschatological vision. Spurgeon explicitly rejects the view that the world will grow worse and end in darkness and idolatry; he insists this prophecy points to the eventual universal worship of God. Calvin sees this as a prediction of the calling of the Gentiles under the Messiah — something David knew of but expressed gently to Jewish ears.

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** “David was not a believer in the theory that the world will grow worse and worse… Not so do we expect, but we look for day when the dwellers in all lands shall learn righteousness.”

**Reformed (Calvin):** The doctrine of Gentile inclusion was unfamiliar to Jewish ears, so David softens it by noting the Gentiles were also created by God.

**Sources:**
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-86.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/86.htm

---

## v. 10 — “For You are great and perform wonders; You alone are God.”

**Traditional reading:** God’s greatness is manifested in His “wondrous things” — miracles of salvation (Kidner, cited by Guzik). The present tense “doest” (KJV) is noted by Spurgeon: God *is doing* wondrous things now, not just in the past. “You alone are God” is an uncompromising monotheistic confession. Spurgeon: “True religion makes no compromises, it does not admit Baal or Dagon to be a god.”

**Sources:**
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-86/
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/86.htm

---

## v. 11 — “Teach me Your way, O LORD, that I may walk in Your truth. Give me an undivided heart, that I may fear Your name.”

**Traditional reading:** This is one of the most beloved verses in the psalm. David shifts from desperate pleas for deliverance to a request for *instruction*. He knows he cannot walk in God’s truth unless God teaches him inwardly by the Spirit. “Unite my heart” (KJV) means “give me an undivided heart” — bring all my scattered affections into one channel directed toward God. The Pulpit Commentary notes that the Hebrew reading (*yached*) has strong manuscript support, meaning “bring all my heart into unison.”

**Baptist (Spurgeon):** “Our minds are apt to be divided between a variety of objects, like trickling streamlets which waste their force in a hundred runnels; our great desire should be to have all our life-floods poured into one channel.”

**Reformed (Calvin):** Two powers are ascribed to free will, but David confesses he lacks both: the light of the Holy Spirit (to overcome blindness of mind) and uprightness of heart (entirely God’s gift). The heart is “scattered about in fragments until God has gathered it to himself.”

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** The united heart is a New Covenant promise (Ezekiel 11:19, “I will give them one heart”), giving believers confidence to pray for it. “Way…truth…unite” foreshadows John 14:6.

**Sources:**
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-86.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/86.htm
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-86/

---

## v. 12 — “I will praise You, O Lord my God, with all my heart; I will glorify Your name forever.”

**Traditional reading:** David vows wholehearted praise with the very “united heart” he has just prayed for. The Pulpit Commentary sees here an implied belief in immortality — praising God “forevermore” requires life beyond death. Spurgeon notes that this is the second time David calls God “my God” (the first was in the agony of v. 2, now in the ecstasy of praise).

**Sources:**
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/86.htm

---

## v. 13 — “For great is Your loving devotion to me; You have delivered me from the depths of Sheol.”

**Traditional reading:** “Loving devotion” is *hesed* — God’s covenant love. The phrase “depths of Sheol” (KJV “lowest hell”) does not imply different levels of the underworld. Lange’s Commentary clarifies that “the underworld” simply refers to the realm of the dead beneath the earth; deliverance means rescue from near-death peril. Calvin explicitly refutes the Roman Catholic use of this verse to support Purgatory: “this argument is too rotten to stand in need of refutation.”

**Reformed (Calvin):** “By the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we are delivered from a still deeper abyss of death” — what David experienced physically, believers experience spiritually through Christ.

**Evangelical (Utley, Bible.org):** The verb “delivered” is a Hiphil perfect, which could be past, present, or future — only context determines. Sheol is the OT holding place of the dead, viewed phenomenologically as in the earth’s centre.

**Sources:**
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-86.html
- https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-86
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/psalms-86.html (via search excerpt)

---

## v. 14 — “The arrogant rise against me, O God; a band of ruthless men seeks my life, with no regard for You.”

**Traditional reading:** The “proud” (*zedim*) are violent, domineering men who act without any fear of God. The Pulpit Commentary notes “they have not set thee before them” means they gave no thought to how God would judge their actions. Calvin observes that those who lack the fear of God will dare any atrocity; the fury of human lusts, unrestrained by reverence for God, knows no limit.

**Baptist (Garner-Howes):** Suggests the historical setting may be Absalom’s revolt.

**Sources:**
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/86.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-86.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/psalms-86.html

---

## v. 15 — “But You, O Lord, are a compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness.”

**Traditional reading:** This is the second direct echo of Exodus 34:6 in the psalm (see v. 5). The “But You, O Lord” creates a sharp contrast with the proud, violent men of v. 14. Spurgeon calls this “a truly glorious doxology, in which there is not one redundant word.” He breaks it down: compassion for the weak, grace for the undeserving, longsuffering for the provoking, mercy for the guilty, truth for the tried. The Pulpit Commentary says the appeal is to God’s own self-revelation: He cannot desert His servant because He has declared Himself to be exactly this kind of God.

**Sources:**
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/86.htm

---

## v. 16 — “Turn to me and have mercy; grant Your strength to Your servant; save the son of Your maidservant.”

**Traditional reading:** “Turn to me” implies that God’s face had seemed averted. “Son of Your maidservant” is a phrase expressing that David is a home-born servant of God — as the child of a slave woman belonged to the master from birth, so David belongs entirely to the Lord. Kretzmann’s Commentary says it means “born into the inheritance of the children of God.” The Pulpit Commentary offers two interpretations: either David’s mother was a specially godly woman, or he means he was born into God’s household as an Israelite.

**Sources:**
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/86.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/psalms-86.html

---

## v. 17 — “Show me a sign of Your goodness, that my enemies may see and be ashamed; for You, O LORD, have helped me and comforted me.”

**Traditional reading:** David asks for a “token for good” — some visible sign that God is dealing with him for good, not evil. The Pulpit Commentary says this need not be a miracle; it is an evidence of divine favour. The purpose is not merely private reassurance but that his enemies might see it and be ashamed. Lange’s Commentary stresses the sign is “not a miracle which the Psalmist implores in order to effect his deliverance” but “an evidence of the Divine favour.” David grounds his request in past experience: “You have helped me and comforted me.”

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik):** Notes that it can be wrong to ask for a sign when the attitude is “prove to me that You love me,” but there are proper times to ask for a “sign for good.” Answers to prayer, preservation of character, deliverance from trouble, joy, forgiveness, confidence, and knowing God’s greatness are all legitimate “signs for good.”

**Sources:**
- https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps086.php
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/86.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lcc/psalms-86.html (via search excerpt)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-86/

---

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Readings

| Tradition | Distinctive Emphasis on Psalm 86 |
|-----------|----------------------------------|
| **Baptist (Spurgeon)** | Vivid, devotional language; stresses perseverance in prayer, the reality of answered prayer over “vain philosophy,” and an optimistic eschatology (v. 9: the nations *will* come to worship). |
| **Reformed (Calvin)** | Emphasises human inability and divine sovereignty. “I am holy/meek” is about innocence relative to enemies, not merit. The heart must be *united* by God alone — a confession that both light and uprightness are gifts, not native to free will. Excludes purgatory (v. 13). |
| **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik)** | Practical, application-oriented. Stresses that God is “ready to forgive *now*,” that the “united heart” connects to New Covenant promises, and that asking for a “sign” can be legitimate when done with right motives. |

- **Gill’s Exposition:** The fetch attempt to biblehub.com failed due to the fetch limit, though the introduction was partially visible in search results — Gill sees David as a type of Christ and notes the psalm may apply to Christ as well as to David.
